notes.meaning: God gives Moses specific court rulings, called judgments, to govern daily life in Israel. These case laws applied the Ten Commandments to real-world disputes between neighbors. They ensured that judges would decide cases with fairness, equity, and the fear of God.

A Hebrew person might become a servant because of extreme poverty or to pay off a debt. Unlike other ancient nations where slavery was permanent, God placed a strict six-year limit on this service. In the seventh year, the servant walked away completely free without paying any fee.

A servant left his master under the same family conditions in which he had entered. If he began his service as a single man, he departed alone. If he was already married when his service began, his wife left with him as a free woman.

If a master gave one of his own female servants to a male Hebrew worker as a wife, that woman remained the master's legal property. Any children born from that union stayed in the master's household when the man's six years ended. The husband was free to leave by himself when his time was completed.

A servant could choose to give up his freedom if he loved his master and wished to stay with his family. His decision had to be spoken clearly and with firm conviction. Rather than facing separation, he could voluntarily choose to remain a bondservant for life.

The master had to bring the servant before the local judges so the choice was made public and official. Then the master took him to a door or doorpost and pierced his earlobe with an awl. This marked the servant as a willing, permanent member of the master's household until death or the year of Jubilee.

When a poor father placed his daughter in another household, it was done with the expectation of marriage rather than ordinary labor. Because her position was tied to family life, she was not simply turned out after six years like a male field hand. The law provided special protections so she would not be cast out into homelessness.

If the master decided not to marry the young woman as planned, he broke trust with her. He was not permitted to sell her to foreigners, who would treat her as an ordinary slave. Instead, he had to allow her own family to buy back her freedom.

If the master gave the young woman to his son instead of marrying her himself, her standing changed completely. She was no longer considered a servant in any sense. The master had to treat her with all the honor and rights of his own daughter.

If a man married another wife, he could not neglect his first wife. He was legally required to keep providing her with adequate food, clothing, and full marital rights. Her marriage was sacred, and taking another spouse did not lessen his duty to care for her.

If the husband failed to honor these basic obligations, the woman was granted immediate release. She walked away as an entirely free woman without paying any money. God protected vulnerable wives from being trapped in neglectful marriages.

Anyone who struck another human being with intent to kill was to be put to death. Because every person is made in God's image, the deliberate taking of human life carries the ultimate penalty. Israel's judges were not allowed to pardon intentional murderers.

God made a clear distinction between deliberate murder and accidental manslaughter. If someone caused a death without planning or malice, God provided a safe haven where the person could run. This protected the accidental killer from being struck down in vengeance by the dead person's family.

A person who planned out a murder in cold blood was granted no mercy. Even if he ran into the sacred tabernacle and grabbed hold of God's altar, the officers were to pull him away and execute him. Holy places were never meant to shield violent criminals from justice.

Striking a father or mother carried the death penalty in ancient Israel. Parents held a sacred position of authority representing God in the home, so physical violence against them showed deep rebellion. God guarded family order by treating an attack on parents as a capital crime.

Kidnapping was strictly punishable by death, whether the victim had already been sold or was still held captive. Stealing a human being destroyed that person's freedom and treated a life like stolen goods. God viewed the slave trade based on kidnapping as an evil worthy of execution.

Speaking a verbal curse against one's parents was also punishable by death. In biblical times, a curse was a solemn wish for someone's ruin or death, showing complete contempt for God-given authority. This rule taught children that honoring parents requires respectful speech as well as obedient actions.

When two men fought and one injured the other with a fist or a stone, the attacker was not charged with murder if the victim survived. The injured person might be confined to bed for a season of recovery. The law stepped in to ensure that violent tempers did not escape legal accountability.

Once the injured man recovered enough to walk outside with a cane, the one who struck him was cleared of any capital charge. However, the attacker had to pay full restitution. He was required to pay for the victim's lost wages and cover all medical expenses until he was completely healed.

If a master beat a servant with a rod and the servant died on the spot, the master faced legal punishment. In many ancient nations, masters could kill servants with total freedom, but God's law declared the servant a protected human life. Cruelty leading to death was treated as a crime before the judges.

If the beaten servant survived for a day or two before dying, the master was not executed. The law presumed the master did not intend to murder the worker, since losing a servant meant losing valuable labor. The financial loss itself served as a heavy penalty when murder could not be proven.

If brawling men struck a pregnant woman and caused an early delivery without lasting harm, the offender was fined. The woman's husband stated the amount of damages, but the court had to approve it to keep it fair. This law protected mothers and their unborn children from reckless violence.

other.view: Some scholars note the ancient Greek translation read this as a fine if the baby was not yet fully formed, while many modern readers take the verse as describing a miscarriage where only the mother's survival prevents a murder charge.

notes.meaning: If serious injury or death resulted from the blow, strict justice was required. The judges were commanded to take a life for a life. This ensured that no one could cause fatal harm to an innocent bystander without facing an equal consequence.

notes.meaning: The principle of an eye for an eye gave judges a standard of exact fairness. It prevented an injured person or family from taking wild, excessive revenge. The punishment had to fit the crime, never exceeding the damage done.

notes.meaning: If an angry master struck a servant and permanently blinded an eye, the master did not receive an eye-for-an-eye injury. Instead, the law commanded that the servant be granted instant, full freedom. Liberty was given as lifelong compensation for the permanent harm.

Knocking out even a single tooth of a servant brought the exact same penalty of freedom. This rule forced masters to control their temper and treat their servants with caution and respect. Harming a worker cost the owner the entire value of that servant's labor.

An ox that gored a person to death had to be stoned, and its meat could not be eaten or sold. The beast was destroyed to show the sacred value of human blood and life. If the animal had never shown dangerous behavior before, the owner was cleared of guilt.

If the ox had a known habit of goring and the owner ignored official warnings to pen it up, the situation was very different. When that neglected animal killed someone, both the ox and its negligent owner faced death. Neglecting known dangers made a person guilty of blood before God and the community.

The court or the victim's family could choose to spare the owner's life by setting a monetary ransom. If this settlement was offered, the owner had to pay whatever amount was demanded to redeem his life. This showed mercy while still holding the careless owner financially responsible.

The same penalty applied whether the gored victim was a grown adult or a young son or daughter. God's law placed the same high value on the lives of children as on adults. Negligent owners could not claim a lesser penalty because the victim was young.

If the dangerous ox killed a male or female servant, the ox was still stoned for taking human life. The owner of the ox was also required to pay thirty silver shekels to the servant's master to replace the loss. This standard payment settled the property loss while the animal's death honored human life.

A person who dug a pit or uncovered an existing cistern was legally required to keep it covered. If he neglected this duty and an ox or donkey fell into the opening, he was held liable for the accident. God expected people to look ahead and prevent hazards that could hurt their neighbors' property.

The owner of the open pit had to make full restitution by paying the neighbor the market value of the lost animal. In return, the pit owner received the carcass of the dead beast to recover whatever value remained. Fair payment restored peace between the two parties.

If an ox with no history of violence unexpectedly attacked and killed a neighbor's ox, the loss was shared equally. Both owners sold the live animal and split the money, and they divided the meat of the dead one. Because neither person was at fault, they bore the unexpected hardship together.

If the ox was known to be dangerous and its owner failed to fence it in, that owner had to pay full compensation. He gave a living ox in place of the dead one and took the carcass for himself. Those who knowingly ignore danger must carry the full cost of the damage they cause.
